summary: This Wikipedia-derived note surveys Zhejiang, an eastern coastal province of China, covering its wartime history under Japanese occupation, its long economic prominence from the Sui and Tang through the Song and Southern Song (with Hangzhou as capital), and its Three Kingdoms-era past. It also describes the province's geography and climate, its religious landscape and recent religious regulation, its administrative divisions, its agricultural and fishing economy, and its post-1949 Communist Party Secretaries.
one_line: Overview of Zhejiang province, China, covering its history, geography, climate, religions, administration, economy and political leaders.
key_facts: During the Second Sino-Japanese War, much of Zhejiang was occupied by Japan and placed under the Reorganized National Government of China, a Japanese puppet state.
The Japanese Imperial Army began the Zhejiang-Jiangxi Campaign to intimidate Chinese civilians out of helping downed American airmen from the Doolittle Raid.
The Japanese killed an estimated 250,000 civilians while searching for Doolittle's men.
In 1999 Zhejiang's Protestant population comprised 2.8% of the provincial population, higher than the national average.
Hangzhou became the capital of the Southern Song under the name Lin'an after the north was lost to the Jurchen Jin dynasty in 1127 following the Jingkang Incident.
Marco Polo called Hangzhou "Kinsay" and claimed it was "the finest and noblest city in the world".
Zhejiang is divided into eleven prefecture-level divisions, 90 county-level divisions, and 1,570 township-level divisions.
Hengdian, belonging to Jinhua, is the largest base of shooting films and TV dramas in China and is called "China's Hollywood".
The Zhoushan fishery is the largest fishery in the country, and Zhejiang is traditionally known as the "Land of Fish and Rice".
Zhejiang has over three thousand islands; Zhoushan Island is Mainland China's third largest island, after Hainan and Chongming.
Zhejiang has a humid subtropical climate with four distinct seasons and annual precipitation of about 1,000 to 1,900 mm.
According to surveys in 2007 and 2009, 23.02% of the population believes in and is involved in cults of ancestors, while 2.62% identifies as Christian.
In mid-2015 the Zhejiang government recognised folk religion as "civil religion", beginning registration of more than twenty thousand folk religious associations.
Tan Zhenlin, the inaugural Party Secretary (term 1949-1952), was one of the leading voices against Mao's Cultural Revolution during the February Countercurrent of 1967.
Of Zhejiang's fourteen Party Secretaries since 1949, none were native to the province.
